body.text: The data identify 37 selected offshore campuses across 13 countries and territories: 26 operating, seven closed and four planned. India has six operating campuses and another three planned, while Malaysia accounts for six current or former ventures. The count excludes education and research centres and partner teaching sites, whose ownership, institutional permanence and degree-delivery arrangements differ from those of offshore campuses.

The status categories matter. Operating campuses show where universities have established a physical offshore presence, while planned campuses reveal where the next round of expansion is being attempted. Closures warn against treating offshore education as an easy substitute for onshore enrolment.

India’s concentration of operating and planned campuses sharpens the irony. Australian universities are bringing their degrees closer to Indian students just as Canberra makes it harder for many of them to bring their families to Australia. India is not covered by the nationality-based exemption available to eligible ASEAN and certain Pacific applicants; Indian applicants must qualify under another exemption, such as doctoral study.

UNSW Asia closed in Singapore in 2007 after enrolments fell far below expectations, despite host-government support. Charles Sturt University’s Ontario campus operated from 2005 until July 2015. Other offshore campuses closed in Malaysia, Fiji, South Africa and Dubai. Monash South Africa operated from 2001 until it was sold in 2019.
These cases show that offshore campuses depend on demand, regulation, partnerships and universities’ willingness to sustain financial and institutional risk.

Nor can they replace the experience of studying in Australia. In 2024, 107,437 students studied Australian higher education courses offshore, compared with 481,851 onshore. Of the offshore group, 47,498 studied at overseas campuses. An Australian degree closer to home can widen access, but it changes where students form friendships, encounter institutions and build professional networks.

Indeed, Canberra is not starting from nothing. Its international education strategy supports diversified offshore delivery, while government agencies advocate for market access and oversee quality. What remains less developed is a strategy covering the full life of these campuses, including why particular ventures merit support, what they should do after opening and how universities should manage withdrawal.

This does not require Canberra to rescue every commercially unviable venture. It requires treating offshore campuses as potential infrastructure for education statecraft, rather than merely as commercially driven extensions of individual universities. They can provide durable places for researchers, students and local institutions to work together. Without a clearer public purpose, however, their contribution to Australia’s regional relationships will remain incidental.

Indonesia already hosts three operating offshore campuses, making it a practical test. The two governments have a framework for higher education and research cooperation. It could support research priorities set jointly by Indonesian and Australian partners and enable more Australian students to study alongside Indonesian peers. Success should be measured not only by enrolments, but also by what local institutions can build and what Australian universities bring back into their own teaching and research.

As Canberra tightens entry to Australia, its universities are taking Australian degrees abroad. That opens markets, though not every venture will survive. It could also sustain relationships across the region, but only if Canberra treats offshore campuses as instruments of education statecraft rather than merely private export ventures. The question is no longer simply where Australian universities open campuses, but what Australia wants them to be for.
